data.title: Nitra – the hillforts of the Principality of Nitra
data.excerpt: From the 8th century Nitra was without doubt the most important agglomeration in the territory of present-day Slovakia, and the early medieval Kingdom of Hungary also took over its exceptional importance. It was the seat of the Principality of Nitra, ruled by Prince Pribina and later by Svatopluk, and six archaeological sites in and around the town document the beginnings of occupation here.
data.metaTitle: Nitra – hillforts of the Principality of Nitra
data.metaDescription: Seat of the Principality of Nitra and the power base of Svatopluk: from the 8th century the most important agglomeration in present-day Slovakia.

keyFacts.label: Number of sites
keyFacts.value: The 6 most important archaeological sites in and around Nitra (Hrad, Martinský vrch, Lupka, Zobor, Mačací hrádok, Šindolka)

keyFacts.label: Area of Martinský vrch
keyFacts.value: 20 ha, fortified with a stone rampart, a ditch and double palisades (posts up to 60 cm in diameter)

keyFacts.label: Area of the Zobor hillfort
keyFacts.value: About 15 ha, three gateways, defences up to 7 m high on the north-west

keyFacts.label: Area of the Lupka hillfort
keyFacts.value: 3.6 ha; rampart 7.5 m high and 3.5 m wide, ditch 3 m deep

keyFacts.label: Rampart of Nitra Castle
keyFacts.value: Total width 5 m — stone walls (1 m) + earthen fill (3 m), reinforced with an oak grillage

keyFacts.label: Church on Martinský vrch
keyFacts.value: 20.1 × 7.6 m, apse 5.4 m, foundation walls up to 1–1.3 m wide

keyFacts.label: The Zobor charter (1111)
keyFacts.value: The oldest surviving charter from the territory of Slovakia — a dispute over the collection of tolls

keyFacts.label: Cemetery by the amphitheatre
keyFacts.value: c. 1,000 graves of the 10th–11th centuries destroyed during construction, only 165 rescued

keyFacts.label: Pottery kilns at Lupka
keyFacts.value: 13 kilns discovered — the first archaeological find of this kind in Slavic territory in the 9th century

timeline.title: The Zobor hillfort is founded
timeline.description: This hilltop hillfort of the Bronze Age was founded by the people of the Lusatian culture in the later phase of the Final Bronze Age.

timeline.title: The Lupka hillfort is founded
timeline.description: An old Slavic hillfort enclosed by a massive stone rampart, guarding the approach to Nitra from the north.

timeline.title: Extensive rebuilding at Nitra Castle
timeline.description: The occupied enclosure on the castle hill was fortified with a massive stone-and-earth rampart of shell construction.

timeline.title: Svatopluk resides in Nitra
timeline.description: Svatopluk resided here as an appanage prince even before his accession to the Great Moravian throne.

timeline.title: Svatopluk’s appanage principality in Nitra
timeline.description: According to the Annals of Fulda, Svatopluk led an appanage principality probably seated in Nitra.

timeline.title: Svatopluk becomes co-ruler with Rastislav
timeline.description: For a certain time Svatopluk became the co-ruler of his uncle Rastislav.

timeline.title: The Conversio Bagoariorum et Carantanorum is written
timeline.description: The first written mention of Nitra and of its ruler Pribina; it was composed at the court of Adalwin, Archbishop of Salzburg.

timeline.title: Svatopluk rules a reunited Nitra and Moravia
timeline.description: After the defeat of the Frankish margraves, the Nitra and Moravian parts of the state were again united under Svatopluk’s rule.

timeline.title: The church on Martinský vrch is consecrated
timeline.description: If this is Pribina’s church, it was consecrated by Archbishop Adalram, who was Archbishop of Salzburg between 821 and 836.

timeline.title: A small church is built at Nitra Castle
timeline.description: It overlies part of an earlier tiered cemetery; its existence supports the assumption of an earlier Great Moravian hillfort.

timeline.title: Fire at the Great Moravian hillfort on the castle hill
timeline.description: An extensive fire interrupted the flourishing of the fortified centre on the castle hill; the precise cause is not known.

timeline.title: A new box rampart is built
timeline.description: New defences of a construction similar to that of the Great Moravian rampart replaced the original fortification of the castle.

timeline.title: Charter of the Zobor abbey
timeline.description: The oldest surviving charter from the territory of Slovakia — in it the abbot of Zobor sues the royal tax collectors.

timeline.title: The prestigious complex at the castle comes to an end
timeline.description: The masonry building (possibly Svatopluk’s seat) came to an end before the north wing of the palace was built.

timeline.title: Štefan Janšák discovers the Lupka hillfort
timeline.description: Janšák described the hillfort and assigned it to geographical category II.

timeline.title: Excavation of the settlement at Šindolka
timeline.description: 32 sunken settlement features and 20 pits of the La Tène period were discovered.

timeline.title: Trial excavation of the Zobor hillfort
timeline.description: Over an area of 14 ares, the probable clay floors of two dwellings and one hearth were identified.

timeline.title: Archaeological excavation on Martinský vrch
timeline.description: After the excavation, parts of the site were conserved at the surface.

timeline.title: A silver radiate-headed fibula found on Zobor
timeline.description: The fibula is dated as early as the 7th century — the first find of its kind from Nitra, published in the AVANS yearbook for 2008.

timeline.title: Zobor as a refuge for the persecuted
timeline.description: During the Holocaust, the vine-growers of Zobor built a modest shelter for the persecuted and supplied them with food.

blocks.text:
Nitra, dear Nitra, Nitra high and proud, where are those days in which you were in flower?
Nitra, dear Nitra, you Slovak mother! When I look upon you, I cannot but weep.
You were once the head of all the lands through which flow the Danube, the Vistula and the Morava.
You were the dwelling of King Svatopluk, when his mighty hand held sway here.
blocks.source: Slovenské Spevy (Slovak Songs), published in Turčiansky Svätý Martin in 1883

children.text: From the 8th century Nitra was without doubt the most important agglomeration in the territory of present-day Slovakia, and the early medieval Kingdom of Hungary also took over its exceptional importance. It was the seat of the Principality of Nitra, where important figures of Slovak national history ruled, above all Prince Pribina (until 833, when he was expelled by the Moravian prince Mojmír) and the prince and later probably king of Great Moravia, Svatopluk, who resided here from as early as the 850s. We first learn of Nitra, and of its first known ruler Pribina, from the work
On the Conversion of the Bavarians and the Carantanians

(Conversio Bagoariorum et Carantanorum), which was probably written between 871 and 873 (elsewhere 828–873 is given) at the court of Adalwin, Archbishop of Salzburg. The work states, among other things:

blocks.text: When, however, some opportunity arose in the meantime, Pribina then, at the request of the faithful men of the aforesaid king, received in fief a certain part of Lower Pannonia around the river called the Sála. He then settled there and began to build a fortified settlement in a marshy grove on the bank of the Sála. He gathered people from all sides and increased the number of his subjects. For him (Pribina) Archbishop Adalram had once consecrated a church on his own estate beyond the Danube, at a place called Nitrava

children.text: Nitra contains the six most important archaeological sites that document the very beginnings of the development of occupation and life in Nitra and its surroundings. Its occupation is of course much older and reaches deep into prehistory. There was a hillfort here, for example, already in the time of the Maďarovce culture.

blocks.caption: The Nitra hillforts
blocks.alt: The Nitra hillforts

children.text: Medieval Nitra was formed by a system of hillforts and, of course, of the settlements belonging to them. A series of excavations in Nitra has made it possible for archaeologists to create a much more precise picture of its appearance at the time when it was the seat of the princes of Nitra in the period of Great Moravia and in the Middle Ages. It really does appear that this was an enormous agglomeration. When the insights we have from the individual smaller excavations in the town are summarised, the importance and uniqueness of that great agglomeration of Great Moravian and post-Great Moravian Nitra is confirmed. It was larger than present-day Nitra and functioned in this state until the 13th century.
On the importance of Nitra, Drahoslav Hulínek states in Historická Revue 11-12 2006 that

“in the period of the Great Moravian state it consisted, besides unfortified settlements of a craft-production or agricultural character, of a hillfort of central importance on the castle hill of Nitra. Part of it was probably also the bailey at Na vŕšku (or else this was a separate hillfort) and two fortified settlements with a possible guard function at the sites of Lupka and Martinský vrch. The originally prehistoric hillfort on the hill of Zobor and the site of Šibeničný vrch may have been used as a refuge.

The core of the Nitra settlement agglomeration was an occupied area of non-agrarian character, represented by the sites of the castle (essentially the whole castle hill), Na vŕšku and the area of today’s Old Town. According to what has been established so far, the Nitra settlement agglomeration contained 18 unfortified settlements and 13 cemeteries of the 9th–10th centuries. According to the Slovak archaeologist Matej Ruttkay, we can state of early medieval Nitra that “the territory of today’s castle (the hillfort of that time) as far as the market hall, and from Fraňa Mojtu Street to Párovská Street, formed one large settlement agglomeration which can without hesitation be compared with the largest Central European metropolises of the day”.

Besides its important political and economic function, Nitra also fulfilled the role of a spiritual centre with a bishopric documented in writing. Within Great Moravia it held a specific position, since it was the most important central settlement of the Nitra part of Great Moravia. Before his accession to the Great Moravian throne, Svatopluk resided here as the appanage prince of the Nitra region. Even after 833 the Nitra region retained a certain autonomy within this West Slavic empire and served as an appanage principality. In keeping with its long-term importance, Nitra also served as the seat of some members of the family of the dynasty ruling over the whole of Great Moravia. This is also shown by the report in the Annals of Fulda on the above-mentioned appanage principality of Svatopluk, probably in Nitra (855?–870). This man was already then an important member of the Mojmír dynasty. Svatopluk, Rastislav’s nephew, was even his co-ruler for some time — from 862/863 if not earlier — already in the 850s, from when he probably ruled in Nitra. Indeed, the Moravian-Pannonian Legends state in the Life of Methodius that Prince Rastislav sent an embassy with a request for Christian teachers and a bishop to the Byzantine emperor Michael together with Svatopluk. This joint action of theirs culminated in the arrival of the Byzantine mission. Among other things, this written source may also point to a certain political recognition of the co-rulership of Svatopluk, who resided in Nitra.

Nitra was probably also the seat of Slavomír, who was in revolt against the Franks. At that time the Moravian part of Great Moravia came, as a result of Frankish domination, into the hands of the margraves of the Eastern March, William II and Engilschalk. After returning to Great Moravia, Svatopluk entered Rastislav’s old stronghold, captured by the Franks — either Mikulčice or, which is less probable, Staré Město — Uherské Hradiště. He secretly joined forces with the rebellious Slavomír, together they crushed Carloman’s army (Carloman, the son of Louis the German), and both Frankish margraves perished. Thanks to this, the Nitra and Moravian parts of the state were again united under a single rule, this time headed by Prince Svatopluk (871–894). The social and political importance of Nitra is further illustrated by the fact that the younger son of Svatopluk I most probably resided here. He was the duke, or prince, of Nitra, Svatopluk II — the opponent of his elder brother Mojmír II, the Great Moravian ruler and successor of Svatopluk I.”

children.text: 1. Nitra — the castle hill

“The dominant seat of the Nitra agglomeration, from the second half of the 9th century at the latest, was the fortified enclosure on the castle hill. The beginnings of its occupation in the Early Middle Ages perhaps reach back as far as the end of the early Slavic period. This is suggested by the few sherds found on the top of the castle hill.

In the second third of the 9th century at the latest, extensive rebuilding took place at the castle. The occupied enclosure on the gentle southern slope of the hill was fortified with a rampart (fig. 3). It consisted of stone walls approximately 1 m wide, built of dry-laid stones, which enclosed an earthen fill approximately 3 m wide (the total width of the rampart was 5 m). The rampart was reinforced by a timber grillage formed of rows of horizontally lying oak beams laid closely side by side, transversely to the course of the defences. The parts of the rampart investigated so far show that the rampart protected not only the northern part of the hill, but the whole occupied enclosure on the castle hill, i.e. including the part today known as the Upper Town.

blocks.caption: The work “On the Conversion of the Bavarians and the Carantanians”
blocks.alt: The work “On the Conversion of the Bavarians and the Carantanians”

children.text: Another important thing was established during the excavation of the rampart. In part of the stone walls of the rampart, building rubble from a dismantled stone masonry structure had been reused. This might indicate that at the time the Great Moravian rampart was built, an earlier stone masonry building that had stood on the top of the hill before the rampart was constructed was dismantled or rebuilt.” (Bednár)

The excavations established that the hillfort originally contained an extensive prestigious building complex — evidently the seat of the prince — which was of masonry and for whose construction very high-quality mortar and ashlars of lithothamnium limestone were used; at the time the complex was built, this stone was quarried in the Leitha Hills in Lower Austria. It is clear from the surviving fragments that the masonry buildings were also decorated with carved plant motifs, and that at least part of the building was plastered and decorated with frescoes. Comparable frescoes come from the surroundings of the three-apsed basilica at Devín. The building came to an end before the north wing of the palace was built, sometime during the 13th century. These could therefore have been the buildings in which Svatopluk himself dwelt.

blocks.caption: Pribina — the first known prince of Nitra
blocks.alt: Pribina — the first known prince of Nitra

children.text: The interior of the hillfort was evidently divided into several parts, as suggested by traces of a palisade inside the feature. Ground-level buildings in which supplies were stored stood immediately against the inner face of the rampart. Besides them, storage pits dug into the ground were also used. The inhabitants of the hillfort probably did not engage in agriculture themselves, and crops were brought to the hillfort already processed, or cleaned. Remains of a metal-casting workshop were recorded at the hillfort. Further finds show that a jeweller’s workshop operated here in the 9th and the early 10th century.

Archaeological excavation as early as the 1930s established that the small church at the castle, today dated to the turn of the 11th and 12th centuries, overlies part of an earlier tiered cemetery. Its existence, together with the situation of the castle hill and the historical sources on the establishment of the bishopric, allows us to assume that the castle was built already as an important Great Moravian hillfort with correspondingly numerous architecture.

blocks.caption: Our visualisation of the possible appearance of the central Nitra hillfort on the castle hill in the period of the Principality of Nitra. Author: Tomáš Humaj.
blocks.alt: Our visualisation of the possible appearance of the central Nitra hillfort on the castle hill in the period of the Principality of Nitra. Author: Tomáš Humaj.

children.text: The most recent excavations at this site have also confirmed that the present-day Church of St Emmeram is not Pribina’s church. The evidence lies beneath the medieval cemetery by the church. The latest results of archaeological excavation and of the geophysical survey carried out with ground-penetrating radar inside the churches standing today suggest a possible location of the Great Moravian church.

Bednár states that “the flourishing of the Great Moravian hillfort on the castle hill was interrupted at an imprecisely determined time by an extensive fire. We record its traces in all the investigated parts of the rampart on the top of the hill. When it broke out and what caused it we do not know. It could have been an unfortunate accident inside the fortified enclosure, but equally a violent intervention from outside. So far we do not have enough finds to determine even approximately when this event occurred. From the finds we do have, we know that it must have happened in the first half of the 11th century at the latest, when new defences with a construction similar to that of the Great Moravian rampart began to be built in the southern part. Their construction was, however, interrupted for reasons so far unknown to us, and only the southern, more accessible part of the hill was fortified. The essential point is that this rampart fulfilled its function until the construction of new defences — the wide box rampart that was built at the castle between 1046 and 1060 (Bednár/Samuel 2001).”

blocks.alt: Reconstruction of the rampart at Nitra — Hrad

children.text: The archaeological excavation of Nitra Castle and the castle hill has produced several convincing proofs of its uninterrupted existence and development from the beginning of the 9th century, and it was established that in the 9th–11th centuries it was the residential seat of the Great Moravian and later the Hungarian principality, and probably also the seat of the Great Moravian bishopric of Nitra. A large amount of indirect evidence for the existence of stone masonry architecture was found on the top of the hill. Its occurrence was concentrated on the top of the castle hill in the area of the palace and the church. At least one of these buildings must have been an extensive, sumptuous and prestigious building complex. This is confirmed, for one thing, by the kind of stone from which it was built — a specific type of limestone that does not occur in the surroundings of Nitra. Its nearest exploited deposits lie approximately 80–100 km from Nitra. In addition, several fragments of plaster with fresco decoration and sumptuously decorated carved architectural elements come from this building, which suggests that a stonemasons’ workshop from the Frankish Empire may have taken part in the construction of this complex.

children.text: Since we know the history of the Principality of Nitra, we know that the site of the original hillfort was permanently occupied and used throughout the Middle Ages, but above all that it was rebuilt several times. It was precisely the many building alterations in the course of the Middle Ages that caused the disturbance, or even the complete destruction, of archaeological features. Today only a tiny fragment of the original hillfort can be seen on the castle hill — part of the rampart with its stone facing. It can be seen in the following picture:

I must state at this point that the enormous potential for presenting this immensely important place in terms of our national history has only begun to be used gradually at Nitra Castle in the last few years. Some four years ago the castle precinct was literally an impregnable fortress for tourists, where it was possible to learn almost nothing about the importance of the place and its history.
2. Nitra — Martinský vrch

blocks.alt: Nitra

children.text: The area was occupied by several cultures already in prehistory. Today the remains of an old Slavic hillfort with an area of 20 ha are visible here. The hillfort was fortified with a stone rampart, a ditch and double massive palisades whose posts were up to 60 cm in diameter. The foundations of a Romanesque church of the 9th century, on which the Church of St Martin grew up in the 11th–12th centuries, were discovered and precisely located at the hillfort. Near the church was a cemetery with valuable finds of the 9th–11th centuries /a Carolingian coin of the 9th century discovered as an obolus of the dead in the mouth of an individual, and dress ornaments of the 11th century/.

In the bailey, several Slavic dwellings were uncovered, as well as a wide /10–12 m/ and long /800 m/ stone road of the 9th century. Numerous grain pits and Slavic craft workshops of the 9th century for producing objects of iron, bone and stone were uncovered here. The village belonging to this church probably lay within the built-up area of the former village of Chrenová.

blocks.alt: Nitra

blocks.caption: Ground plan and probable appearance of the church
blocks.alt: Ground plan and probable appearance of the church

children.text: The church mentioned was of masonry, had foundation walls up to 1–1.3 m wide, and was 20.1 m long and 7.6 m wide, with an apse of 5.4 m. Small remains of plaster reveal coloured fresco decoration in the church. In the foundations of this old church, jewellery and the grave of an adult were found; the person had in their mouth a coin of the period of Charles the Bald (840–877). It is possible that this was Pribina’s church, mentioned in the historical documents, but direct evidence for this claim does not exist. If that were true, the church was built sometime between 821 and 836, because those are the years when Adalram was Archbishop of Salzburg, and we know from the historical reports that Adalram consecrated this church. (The most probable years are 827–828.) The technique of building the church’s foundations is similar to that of the church revealed at Bratislava Castle and also of the church at Blatnohrad (today’s Zalavár in Hungary), which Pribina later had built in his principality in Pannonia. All this would mean that the hillfort on Martinský vrch, on the hillside of Zobor, was Pribina’s seat, where he may also have had a princely palace. An archaeological excavation was carried out in the area in 1993. Parts of the site were conserved at the surface. Today this area belongs to the Ministry of Defence of the Slovak Republic and is not accessible to the public.
3. Nitra — Lupka

This old Slavic hillfort, enclosed by a massive stone rampart of the 8th–9th century, was founded by the Slavs of the Great Moravian period. It guarded the approach to Nitra from the north. Besides the enclosure proper, protected by a stone rampart 7.5 m high and 3.5 m wide and by a ditch 3 m deep on the inner side, it also had a fortified extensive outer settlement at the southern foot of the hill. To the north-west, below the partially preserved rampart, a terrace 6 m wide was laid out and pottery kilns were built into it.
Štefan Janšák discovered the hillfort in 1928 and writes the following about it

: The hillfort lies halfway between the town of Nitra and the village of Dražovce, about 3 km from each, and roughly 100 m above the level of the county road mentioned. It forms the last south-western spur of the Zobor mountain massif, which here passes into the valley plain of the river Nitra. In its geographical form the hillfort belongs to category II, extending over a hill of an almost regular loaf-like shape, which on the north-eastern side is connected by a flat saddle to the massif of Zobor.

blocks.alt: 3D reconstruction of the church according to the Institute of Archaeology SAS

children.text: The hillfort is composed of Triassic layers of variegated sandstone and marl. The natural defensibility of the hillfort is slight and can be spoken of only on the eastern side, where there is a steep rocky step 3–4 m high over a length of about 100 m, between the two quarries L and M. This is probably a kind of distant bailey of Zobor, or a station for a more numerous guard, and therefore neither natural defensibility nor artificial fortifications are required here on such a large scale as at permanently inhabited hillforts. The artificial ramparts form an almost regular ellipse with axes differing little in length. The ramparts were created by digging away a fairly wide strip on the inner side of the hillfort, so that they have no parallel ditch which would increase the solidity of the defences. The height of the ramparts is 0.80–1 m towards the interior of the hillfort, and 2 m, at most 3 m, outwards, and their length (circumference) is 680 m. Today the ramparts are considerably flattened, which must also be attributed to the circumstance that in the sections in d and c they serve as a promenade path for Nitra’s trippers. The lowest point of the ramparts is spot height 225 at point c, from where they rise in both directions until at point b they reach spot height 337 and tower above a rocky step 4 m high. The ramparts are interrupted in two places by the quarries L and M. Besides this, entrances have been broken through them in several places, evidently of a later date. Entrance o on the south-eastern side provides a comfortable ascent to the hillfort.

blocks.alt: Nitra

children.text: The surface area amounts to 3.6 ha. Given its shape and the fact that the surface slopes equally towards all points of the compass, no part of the hillfort offers any special advantages, either for habitation or in terms of safety.

The kilns had a lower heating area and an upper firing area; they date from the 9th century. In the whole area a large quantity of high-quality Old Slavic pottery of this period was found, made on fast-rotating potter’s wheels, which testifies to the great skill of our ancestors in the potter’s craft. The pottery was decorated with a beautiful fine wavy line between bundles of fine and stronger grooves. To the south-east of the kilns, towards the town, below the rampart itself, there was a smaller cemetery in which the first potters — craftsmen — so far known from the territory of present-day Slovakia were buried. This is a valuable Great Moravian cemetery whose finds testify to an advanced jeweller’s craft: complex types of earrings, finger rings and small gombíky of gold, silver and bronze. The hillfort served as a refuge for the surrounding population in times of military danger; otherwise a smaller garrison was stationed here, protecting the approach road to the princely hillfort from this side. A few years ago a find spot containing 13 pottery kilns, small kilns without a grate and so on was uncovered here. The pottery kilns at the Lupka hillfort are the first archaeological find of this kind in Slavic territory in the 9th century. Today the ramparts of the defences are still clearly visible in the forest growth and the whole site is at the same time a nature reserve for plants.

4. Nitra — Zobor

A hilltop hillfort of the Bronze Age (the Lusatian culture) and of the Middle Ages (the 9th century). It is the first fortified hilltop settlement in the Nitra valley and, with its area of about 15 ha, it is among the largest in this region. The defences encircle the entire crown of the massif, both the Pyramída and the summit of Zobor proper, which are separated from each other by a pronounced saddle. The height of the defences on the north-western side reaches about 7 m. The hillfort was entered through three gateways, placed in the eastern, northern and western part of the rampart. Given its dominant position and its area, the hillfort in the period of the Lusatian culture is thought to have fulfilled, besides serving as a refuge for the inhabitants of the surrounding hamlets, an organisational and administrative or a cult function.

blocks.caption: Great Moravian earrings from Nitra — Lupka
blocks.alt: Great Moravian earrings from Nitra — Lupka

children.text: The origin of the Zobor hillfort is dated to the Final Bronze Age (10th to 8th century BC). The earliest occupation of the Zobor hillfort (hereafter ZH) is linked to the people of the Lusatian culture (hereafter LC), who in the later phase of the Final Bronze Age built extensive hillforts of the upland type. Occupation here lasted until the beginning of the Early Iron Age (the Hallstatt period), when the hillforts and open hamlets of the LC came to an end (according to one hypothesis this was caused by the arrival of mounted warrior retinues from the area of the Pontic steppes and the northern Caucasus). The question of the occupation of the ZH in the period of Great Moravia remains unanswered. In this period the earlier fortification could have been used as a refuge (a place of refuge) and a lookout point. The most recent finds from Zobor, however, suggest that
the occupation of Zobor can also be shifted to the Slavic period
. Found here (published in the AVANS yearbook for 2008) was a
silver radiate-headed fibula

, dated as early as the 7th century. The radiate-headed fibula is the first find of its kind from Nitra, even though more settlements and graves of this period have been identified in the town’s territory in the past. The quality of the find underlines the importance of this agglomeration just beyond the northern limit of the distribution of Avar cemeteries. Other early medieval finds, published in 2008, had likewise been recorded only in limited quantities at the site during the excavations so far. While a
knife with a marked groove
below the edge of the blade is among ordinary products,
long knives with a straight, narrow and massive blade
are found rather in Avar cemeteries. Important is the specimen with a volute-ended
decorated handle
. According to the observations of several researchers, this characteristic tool appears over the long period of the 6th–9th centuries.

children.text: The Zobor hillfort had a strategic position; it was the first buffer hillfort from the area of the lower Nitra region, with a good and wide outlook and with the possibility of observing and controlling a large territory. It was part of a chain system of hillforts which fulfilled a signalling, defensive and communication function. The nearby hillforts of Žibrica, Veľký Lysec, Veľký Tríbeč and Krnča-Tábor also belonged to it. The defences of the ZH and the difficult terrain provided, in times of threat, a refuge for the inhabitants of the surrounding open hamlets on the slopes of Zobor and in the Nitra valley (for example the hamlets in the area of the St Svorad Specialised Hospital, at Šindolka, or above Nitrianske Hrnčiarovce), which formed its economic hinterland. In addition, the ZH probably also had functions of an organisational and administrative, an economic and a cult character. The defensive rampart itself consisted of a fill of stone and earth, which was reinforced in its lower part by a timber construction. On the crest of the rampart stood a palisade of wooden posts. On the inner side of the rampart a depression is visible along almost its entire length, created by extracting material for its construction.

blocks.caption: The ramparts are where it is now thoroughly overgrown and hard to photograph; what is a little further off can no longer be seen.
blocks.alt: The ramparts are where it is now thoroughly overgrown and hard to photograph; what is a little further off can no longer be seen.

children.text: The three entrances to the hillfort were formed by partly pincer-shaped gates, and the original period roads led into them. Today the red waymarked trail, which is at the same time a vehicle road, leads into the western gateway. The blue waymarked trail from Lyžiarska lúka leads into the northern gateway. A forest haulage road to Nitrianske Hrnčiarovce passes through the eastern gateway. The gates were of wood, probably doubled, strongly fortified and coupled with a watchtower.

The surroundings of the hillfort were cleared of forest for tactical reasons, for a better view, and also in order to use the wood for fuel and building material. In the wider surroundings there are further, less discernible defensive ramparts which protected the approaches to the hillfort at the most accessible places.

Inside the hillfort there were probably wooden dwellings and farm and storage features for keeping food. The archaeological excavations carried out so far have not confirmed an increased concentration of settlement features. A cistern for collecting rainwater was created by damming a gully with the defensive rampart in the western part of the hillfort. On the basis of parallels from other hillforts we can assume that the summit of Zobor, as a natural dominant feature of the terrain, was probably the acropolis for the people of the LC, reserved for the highest stratum of a socially differentiated society.

blocks.caption: View from below of the highest rampart
blocks.alt: View from below of the highest rampart

children.text: The archaeological excavation and its finds date the origin of the Zobor hillfort to the Final Bronze Age. Most of the finds consisted of fragments of pottery vessels, and only a small number were metal objects (a bronze spearhead, two small iron knives and fragments of bronze objects). A long-known find is a socketed bronze axe. Trial archaeological excavation in 1986–1987 identified, over a total investigated area of 14 ares, what are most probably the clay floors of two dwellings and one hearth. The Zobor hillfort and its immediate surroundings provided a refuge not only for people in ancient times, but also for those persecuted during the Second World War and the Holocaust. The vine-growers of Zobor built them a modest shelter, supplied them with food here and helped them to survive. Several were helped across the border via the Nitra airfield.

The oldest surviving charter from the territory of Slovakia is also connected with Zobor — the so-called charter of the Zobor abbey of 1111, in which the abbot of Zobor sues the royal tax collectors for seeking to deprive the abbey of its rights to collect tolls in the area of Nitra, the Váh and Trenčín. The charter records several names of respected citizens of Nitra who took part in the court hearing. Some of them are over 80 years old. The senior court official has a Slovak name, as does the canon, and of all the names mentioned 14 are Slovak, 4 are German and the rest are generally Christian.

children.text: 5. Nitra — Mačací hrádok

It is a valuable Roman-period and hillfort-period archaeological site as well as a medieval small fort with iron and glass production. The site is dated to the 12th–13th centuries. The archaeological excavation identified its own outer settlement with important craft smithing production, as well as an extensive cemetery accompanied by simple jewellery. The terrain was also advantageous for defending the enclosure of the hillfort. It was fortified with double massive palisades, the individual posts being up to 60 cm in diameter. The houses mostly had stone footings. The site is also a rich find spot of various stone objects such as axes with a drilled hole, fragments of flints, pieces of flat, well-smoothed small pots and others. Various iron objects, vessels, hoops and the like were also found here.
6. Nitra — Šindolka

blocks.caption: A terrace with a rampart
blocks.alt: A terrace with a rampart

children.text: A large-scale site with finds of a multi-period settlement, with occupation predominating in the Middle La Tène period and in the Middle Ages. In the Middle La Tène period there was a settlement at Šindolka which is among the largest settlements so far investigated in Slovakia. Between 1968 and 1995, 32 sunken settlement features and 20 pits were discovered. The basic building material was wood and clay. The walls of the huts were either of logs or wattled from withies and filled with clay, which has survived as daub. Little has survived of the interior fittings of the buildings. Mostly they are clay projections which we take to be benches. Some buildings also had a production, a farming or a combined function, so that the space was divided into a living, a working and a storage part. The pits had a storage or possibly an extraction function. The archaeological finds comprise bronze and iron fibulae, glass and lignite bracelets and small iron objects. Cremation graves uncovered by the excavation date from the La Tène period and are probably the remnant of a cemetery.

In the Middle Ages there was a settlement and cemeteries at Šindolka. In the 9th–10th centuries there was a farming and craft hamlet here, and in the 11th–13th centuries a medieval village which, however, is not identified in the written sources. The archaeological excavation uncovered dwelling features with stone and clay ovens, production features, ovens sunk into the ground, and storage and refuse pits. Within the settlement area, graves of the 10th–11th centuries were found, some of which contained Árpád coins, S-shaped temple rings, glass beads, silver finger rings and a bronze finger ring.

Many finds in Nitra prove that after the demise of old Moravia Nitra did not die out but continued to be densely occupied. During the construction of the open-air amphitheatre, a large Old Slavic cemetery of the 10th to 11th centuries was destroyed, where the graves were neatly oriented in rows, and it is assumed that there may have been about 1,000 of them here. The construction workers destroyed almost everything; only 165 graves were rescued, with various grave goods but also with jewellery that had been made in Nitra. There must have been a large settlement nearby, and in this old cemetery there must have been some ecclesiastical building or a church, perhaps built as early as the 9th century. It is clear that our ancestors did not appear here only in the 10th century, even though the objects found in the graves — and therefore also the people buried in them — were of the 10th to 11th centuries. Only a small part of the cemetery was rescued, however; the older part was probably destroyed together with the foundations of the church. The assumed size of the burial ground also reveals that burial must have been taking place here for a long time already. Unfortunately, these assumptions can no longer be either confirmed or refuted, since the construction company saw to the complete destruction of almost the entire site.

children.text: In the surroundings of Nitra there are a great many sites where various Old Slavic archaeological finds of the first millennium have been made. The great majority of these finds come merely from rescue excavation of the given site after it had been disturbed by some building activity. These are therefore entirely chance finds without further systematic excavation. Even so, we can see the great density of occupation of this area by our ancestors from the 5th century onwards.
